title: Leonce's quick ear and listening to Black bands
summary: Leonce, called the professor, learned by listening to the Imperial and Superior bands, and played a funeral by ear, even opera, without reading music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Colored that was with a beating heart with a colored folks. They used to have a dance every Saturday night. L-I-V-A had to get all that stuff because L-I-V-A had to have to hit a piece twice or three times before I could play it. But then L-I-V-A had to hit that thing once. Lance, Lance, he'd hit that thing once. Boy, he might make one or two humbugs on it, but he ain't gonna make too many humbugs. He had a quick ear and a good ear. I mean a real good ear. Did you tell me one time that he used to go around to some of the joints where the neighbors were playing? Yeah, yeah, yeah. They taught Lance as a professor. They taught Lance as a professor. Do you remember who he heard around at those places? Well, he used to hear the Imperium and Superior. That was the only two bands that really prayed. Back in the Red Light District, Eddie Souchon, everyone Souchon said that he named the men that they had a Tom Anderson. Tom Anderson's band was composed of a bass, a violin, a guitar, and a vowel trombone, a tenor trombone. That's what Tom Anderson had. And Lance would go around there and listen to all them fellas. They used to call Lance the professor. Alan wanted him to teach his trombone player how to play music. Who is that, Alan? Nigga Allen from Dretton. And we was over the river a couple of times and they'd come over there and they'd be listening, you know, listening to Lance by Trumbo. That's the one there. I was up at the Louis Cresson's some years ago and Manny Perez's wife, he used to be the trumpet player for the Imperial Office, the colored man. And I went to Louis Cresson and says, Mello, he says, you know who this woman is? I says, I do not. He says, that's Manny Perez's wife. And Louis Cresson says to Manny Perez's wife, the other nigga, says, that's Mello, the trumpet player. He says, well, Manny never said much. He only was a good trumpet player. He said, but he sure knew Lyle. He sure knew Lyle. Lyle would go around there, steal all of these music and come back and play it. Oh, it was a case. I just liked to hear Lyle play Frumbo than somebody else. I could just hear the parts that he put in, you know, God told him. And he had the knack of putting them in. He had the knack of putting them in. And he knew when and how and what time. So, we had Jacqueline tell you about this. Played a funeral procession over there. And he said, who you got in the lineup? I said, well, he said, we're going to use the old wire face. There he goes, that was old man Alessandro. And his son, Manuel, used to call him Little Wire Face. He says, we're going to use Alessandro on tuba. He says, we'll use Brock on barbond. He said trombone. I said, Lyle. He looked at me. I said, Lyle. It's all right. So, we had Joe Castro and Joe Castro and Little Wire Face, they're going out to us. With them old, that Little Dago had one of them rotary valves. You ever see them old Dago horns, rotary valves? They got good action to him. He said, all right. We started off, man. We tore them up going to the where the old throw was laid out. and got there, played the piece, played the Nero of my God, when they took them out. And then when when we started off, and we got a half a block away, we started off going to the church. old Jack Lennon. I said, what's the matter? He said, he played it. He pressed me on the bus. Well, Lyle's had the knack. He had the knack to play that kind of music. Lyle's playing the kind of music. He'd play opera. He couldn't read a note. He'd play opera and he couldn't read a note.
